title: 1Password data breach included some customer info, internal source code
summary: 1Password is reassuring customers that their password vaults are safe after the theft of both account records for a subset of its users and source code from its private repositories. The company said it began investigating the incident on November 19, after it detected indications that an employee’s corporate GitHub account had been breached. The attacker used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded what 1Password described as “administrative data” about a subset of users. This included customer names and email addresses, account and user IDs, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters, and “other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture.” Tokens used in some emailed links to customers inviting them to accept provisioning invitations or account recovery were also stolen, although 1Password said that these tokens must be combined with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit confirmation code sent to the user’s registered email address before account access is granted. The company has notified affected customers and, to further secure authentication, has changed the confirmation code format from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and accessed the continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) system; while 1Password said that the source code contained no user secrets, infrastructure secrets in the CI/CD system may have been exposed. The company has triggered a rotation of all relevant credentials. Vaults not affected However, it emphasized, customers’ password vaults were not affected, nor were the keys that protect them. The company also pointed out that it does not store account passwords or secret keys; customers are the only ones who have keys to their vaults. title: Code-driven AI illustrations are more useful than images from dedicated image models
summary: An interesting trend in frontier LLMs released in the second half of 2026 is that they tend to be much better at visual reasoning and creative "design" than their predecessors. If you ask these text-output models to create a 2D image (or a 3D model, as discussed here previously ), you're very likely to get a useful result, and you may even get one that's aesthetically impressive. Most importantly, because these images are defined using code you (or the model) can make further edits to them without any of the weirdness that comes from iterating with a text-input, image-output model. Poster design with Gemini 4 Neon Gemini 4 Neon is getting some buzz for its 2D design skills, so I decided to try it out in AI Studio starting with the prompt: Create an SVG poster promoting the Kakapo recovery project, research details first, make the poster look really cool and give it a 1970s graphic design It took some iteration, partly because AI Studio doesn't render SVGs, so the models there can't spot visual mistakes without assistance. Make the kakapo a bit more realistic, especially the face (image search for references) Then: [IMAGE] The text here doesn't fit the pill, fix it And: [IMAGE 2], [IMAGE 3] Also these Here's the full transcript , exported from AI Studio as Markdown because I couldn't find a way to share a session that didn't require a Google login to view. The end result is pretty solid: AI Studio ran Google searches to find those numbers - I've checked and they are all correct. I like that it included red rimu tree fruit on the branch, since those are essential for the breeding season . Whether or not you like the poster, the key thing about it is that everything is editable . You can directly edit the text in the SVG, or you can open it in Inkscape or Adobe Illustrator or Boxy SVG and edit it visually.
